content: Queen Alexandra's Royal Naval Nursing Service (QARNNS) serves as the nursing branch of the British Royal Navy. Its personnel collaborate closely with the Royal Navy Medical Branch. As of January 1, 2006, according to Don Touhig, a former junior minister of the Ministry of Defence, QARNNS comprised 240 Naval Nurses and 90 Nursing Officers. In 1883, a committee identified the need for improvements in medical and nursing care within the Royal Navy. Consequently, in 1884, a uniformed Naval Nursing Service was established, staffed by trained nurses. These nurses initially served onshore at locations such as Haslar and Plymouth. In 1902, Alexandra of Denmark, the queen consort of Edward VII of the United Kingdom, became President of the Nursing Staff. In her honor, the Naval Nursing Service was renamed Queen Alexandra's Royal Naval Nursing Service. A reserve branch of QARNNS was created on October 13, 1910. During the First World War in 1914, QARNNS expanded significantly, with numerous volunteers from the British Red Cross and civilian hospitals joining the service. Similarly, during the Second World War, many volunteer QARNNS nurses were deployed overseas. In 1949, a nursing branch of the Women’s Royal Naval Service (WRNS) was formed, but in 1960, these nurses were integrated into QARNNS, creating a unified nursing service. In 1982, the service became integrated, allowing men to serve as nurses in QARNNS. The first male nurse to join was Senior Nursing Officer Rajendrasen Purusrum, who was commissioned on March 1, 1983. Although QARNNS was fully affiliated with the Royal Navy from 1977, it remained technically a separate service until March 31, 2000, when it officially became part of the Royal Navy. Queen Alexandra served as President until her death in 1925, after which she was succeeded by Queen Mary in 1926. Princess Alexandra became Patron of QARNNS in 1955. Initially, QARNNS had only two ranks: Nursing Sister and Head Sister. In 1911, the intermediate rank of Superintending Sister was introduced. The service did not have an overall head until the rank of Head Sister-in-Chief was established on August 1, 1927. By 1937, the titles Head Sister and Head Sister-in-Chief were changed to Matron and Matron-in-Chief, respectively. The ranking system underwent changes during the Second World War. In 1960, with the integration of WRNS nurses, ratings known as Naval Nurses were introduced, and their ranking system mirrored that of Royal Navy ratings. In 1982, in preparation for the inclusion of male officers, the Nursing Officers' ranking system was revised. In 1995, QARNNS transitioned to using Royal Navy ranks.
